newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Delayed IMF loan clouds Russian eurobond.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Delayed IMF loan clouds Russian eurobond.

text.p: Investors are lining up to buy Russia's first eurobond, but a cloud of uncertainty remains as to when the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will pay out a delayed tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia.
"The situation is difficult. We have problems," Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said, when asked about the IMF talks.
Fund officials were more cautious. "I can't really say anything," said Tom Wolf, IMF resident representative in Moscow. "We're still in the process of making our assessment."
Wolf said an IMF mission would work until Monday instead of leaving at the end of this week as previously planned.
"It's going to be an extremely difficult call," added a source close to the talks.
A Fund mission left Moscow last month without deciding whether to recommend that the next tranche of the three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) should be paid out.
The IMF was particularly worried at Russia's poor tax collection performance and said it wanted to see an improvement in revenues before paying out the next installment of the loan.
More importantly, the IMF wants evidence the improvement is sustainable and not just the result of a one-off push.

The IMF delayed a tranche in July because of tax revenue worries, and released it in August because preliminary revenue data for the month showed an improvement. But the final data for August were not as good as the initial figures had suggested.
The Finance Ministry says tax revenues have improved sharply since they started to get tough on tax arrears in August and threatened in October to bankrupt major tax debtors.

Revenues in September were 11 trillion roubles ($2 billion) according to preliminary data, but 13.5 trillion according to final data. They picked up to 17 trillion in October and were running at a monthly rate of 25 trillion -- or 12 percent of gross domestic product -- in the first 20 days of November.

"Five weeks before the end of the year, Russian finances are soundly on track in spite of the costs of political uncertainty throughout 1996," said Jochen Wermuth, head of the Finance Ministry's Economic Expert Group.
But even if the IMF is persuaded that matters are improving, they may want to wait longer before deciding to pay up.

"They've got to demonstrate a track record over a longer period of time," said a source close to the talks. "Even if there's a positive assessment there won't be any money coming until some time in December."
That is in line with the picture painted by the Russian authorities, who have been keen to play down expectations.

The respected Sevodnya Daily newspaper said on Tuesday the Fund's board would not decide whether to pay the October or November tranches until December, so Russia would not receive the money until next year.
The success of the eurobond, launched on Thursday, is timely as the IMF problems mean at least $650 million of credits budgeted for this year may not be paid until 1997.
The debut eurobond was heavily oversubscribed, despite a volume of $1 billion instead of the $500 million expected at the start of this month's international roadshow.
The eurobond was priced at a tight 3.45 percentage points over U.S. treasuries, with a longer than expected five-year maturity.
"If they think the markets are going to give them a good price and they can float more, then why not, especially as there's this uncertainty with the IMF money," said one source.
"This money comes without conditions."

Troubles with the IMF will not be over with this tranche. Economy Minister Yasin said the programme for next year would have to be renegotiated to take into account changes in the economy since the EFF was agreed in February this year.
But the international investment community seems unbothered, with the European credit rating agency IBCA reaffirming its BB+ long-term rating on the eurobond after the terms were published.
($1=5495 Rouble)
